..
Issued at 100 AM MDT Thu Oct 22 2026

IR continues to depict ample cloud cover extending from the
eastern Pacific, bringing in tropical moisture through much of
the Rockies and pushing to the north. There has been a bit
further eastern push of this moisture, and as such, any shower
activity looks to be more along and east of the Divide extending
from Sweetwater to Natrona Counties throughout the day Thursday.
Impacts negligible at this time, brining in continued needed 
precipitation chances in the coming days. WV shows the main 
finger of the PFJ pushing further south across the Pacific 
northwest and extending into southern Canada. The closed low has
pushed across southern California with its eastern progression 
starting as it nears the CWA and upper Rockies later Thursday. 
This will interact with the aforementioned tropical moisture 
that will provide better precipitation chances on Friday.

Winds will increase late Thursday morning as the gradient starts
to strengthen ahead of this system, seeing southwest wind gusts
up to 25 to 35 mph across the Wind Corridor, and 20 to 30 mph
for other areas east of the Divide. 15 to 25 mph expected to the
west, but the stronger wind comes late Friday morning and into
the afternoon and evening hours. Winds remain elevated overnight
Thursday, but the strongest winds up to 40 to 60 mph expected,
highest from South Pass to outer drive of Casper Mountain, where
an occasional higher gust is possible. Regardless, the main
concern comes with frontal pass late Friday afternoon and into
the evening hours out of the west to northwest behind it. Winds
slowly diminish with the wind shift change but remain elevated
for 2 to 3 hours behind FROPA before becoming relatively light
overnight. Winds across northern Natrona and much of Johnson,
will stay elevated through sun-up Saturday morning before
becoming relatively light. 

Precipitation wise, Thursday will see isolated shower activity,
with the best chances for Sweetwater and Natrona Counties into
the afternoon and early evening hours. A rumble of thunder
cannot be ruled out with instability values up to 100-200 J/kg
expected but much of this activity will be east into the CYS
CWA. This will help aid the stronger winds as well with any
outflows with this shower activity, but minimal impacts (if any)
will be expected. Increasing chances come Friday morning with
first wave of moisture coming out of eastern Idaho and northern
Utah pushing into the west by sunrise. An isolated storm is
possible with any stronger outflows the main hazard. Snowfall
looks to be minimal for the highest of the peaks along and west
of the Divide, through mid to late morning with dry conditions
expected to the east. The next round of shower activity will
come with frontal passage as the cold front pushes into
Yellowstone by 3 to 5PM and pushing southeast and through the
CWA by midnight. This is when freezing levels look to drop
between 8-9kft, allowing for snow to fall across the higher
terrain of the western mountains, and as well as the Bighorns.
Minimal impacts expected for the Bighorns as models have
diminished in QPF amounts, with the passes looking to stay
minimally impacted at this time. West of the Divide will be a
different story, even through less snowfall now likely. Teton
and Togwotee has the best chances for a couple of inches to fall
late Friday afternoon into the overnight hours (30-40%) with
anything higher in elevation pushing up to 6 inches (50-60%).
This could continue its downward trend, and as such, even
advisory level snowfall does not look to be great at this time.
This is following in line with last winter with systems that
look good a few days out, looking to weaken as it nears the CWA
before models do anything good on how it turns out. This could
be a pre-cursor of the winter to come, especially with the
stronger El-Nino expected as well. 

As this more open wave progresses northeast and gets embedded
back into the jet stream for the northern Dakotas, another
trough begins to deepen along the Pacific Northwest out of the
Gulf of Alaska with increasing divergence aloft. This begins to
near the CWA by late Sunday and into early next week with a
better track for the western mountains for any significant
snowfall. Again, time will tell as we are finding out currently
and from last winter. If anything, it will reinforce the colder
air from this late work week system with more seasonable to just
below average temperatures heading into the last week of
October. In all, a more active pattern has commenced with more
fall like weather as the jet gets closer and closer with its
southward and standard progression (even if a month late).
